patient_information: A 36-year-old male restaurant owner presented for assessment. He is married and took malaria chemoprophylaxis for his recent travel. His HIV antibody test was negative.
chief_complaint: A mobile itchy mass under the skin for three weeks.
history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to presentation, the patient first noted a mass in his groin which lasted for 4 days before subsiding. Following this, he developed an itchy, serpiginous rash that tracked from his groin to his chest over several days and then disappeared. The mass then reappeared on his right shoulder, prompting him to seek assessment. He reported no history of fever or systemic illness.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Five weeks before presentation, the patient returned from a fishing holiday in the Okavango Delta in Botswana with four friends. During the trip, he slept on a boat under a mosquito net, swam in fresh river water, and ate freshwater fish from the river. He later admitted that they had made and consumed sushi from fresh fish caught in the river. Two of the four friends who accompanied him developed the same complaint, indicating a common source exposure.
physical_exam: On his right upper deltoid, there was a firm mass with clear margins, 3x8 cm in size. A serpiginous tract was visible, tracking from the mass across his upper chest wall. The remainder of the organ system examination was normal, with no additional rash and no lymphadenopathy.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory results showed a normal total white cell count of 8.9 x 10^9/L but a significant eosinophilia with an eosinophil count of 0.9 x 10^9/L (reference <0.5). Liver function tests, creatinine, and electrolytes were normal. Serology for Gnathostoma was negative. The diagnosis was confirmed when the patient expressed a larva from his nostril, which was identified as Gnathostoma spinigerum.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential diagnosis included other parasitic causes of migratory swelling and eosinophilia. Loa loa infection (calabar swelling) was considered but was unlikely as it is not endemic in the Okavango Delta and has a minimum incubation period of 5 months. Sparganosis, another rare cause, typically occurs in Asia. Other creeping eruptions, such as those from animal hookworms (cutaneous larva migrans) or Strongyloides stercoralis, were less likely as they present with fine, serpiginous tracks rather than a large mobile mass.
management_and_clinical_course: A clinical diagnosis of cutaneous gnathostomiasis was made, and the patient was started on albendazole 400mg twice daily for 21 days and a single dose of ivermectin 200 mcg/kg. Over the next six days, the lesion migrated over his shoulder, neck, disappeared for 24 hours, and then reappeared between his eyebrows, moving across his forehead and face before being felt inside his nose. On the sixth day of treatment, he successfully expressed the larva from his nostril. His two symptomatic friends received similar treatment with full resolution of their symptoms.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was cutaneous gnathostomiasis caused by the nematode Gnathostoma spinigerum. This was established based on the classic clinical presentation of a migratory subcutaneous mass and serpiginous rash, significant peripheral eosinophilia, and a clear epidemiologic link of eating raw freshwater fish in an endemic area. The diagnosis was definitively confirmed by the physical recovery and identification of the G. spinigerum larva from the patient's nostril during treatment.
